source.basis: Operator spec page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
CyrusOne's Austin AUS2-AUS3 campus publishes 19 MW of IT load across 242,000 square feet, tenth by capacity among the 19 Texas facilities that disclose a figure.

The denominator matters more than the rank. Texas has 133 mapped data center facilities, and only 19 publish any capacity at all. This campus's 4 percent share of the state's 475 MW of disclosed IT load is a share of a disclosed subset, not of Texas supply. The standing says as much about who reports as about who is large.

The certifications are the clearest signal of intended use. PCI DSS, HIPAA, ISO 27001, FISMA, SSAE 16 Type II and TIA-942 point to financial, healthcare and federal workloads, which carry compliance obligations that unconstrained AI training does not. A campus built to those standards is not automatically the cheapest place to put a GPU cluster.

For AI specifically, 19 MW is a ceiling on IT load, not a measure of what is available. The data does not publish power delivery headroom, the rack density the electrical and cooling systems can support, or the quality of grid interconnection, and those are the constraints that decide whether a site can absorb modern accelerator racks. The suitability score of 62 is computed from published IT capacity and operator type alone, and the one input it flags as missing is announced expansion.

Several fields are empty: no street address, no coordinates, no nearest airport. The 40 kW per rack figure used to convert 19 MW into roughly 475 racks is a stated assumption, not an operator specification. Nothing here establishes when the capacity was built, how much is leased, or what is drawing power today.

suitability.basis: weighted mean of the published inputs named here, scaled to 100; formula on the methodology page
